summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults was decriminalised by the High Court in Jones v Attorney General in 2018, a ruling upheld on appeal. The challenge was brought by the activist Jason Jones, who stated publicly during the proceedings that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner, the maximum exposure under the criminal provisions then in force. Decriminalisation removed the threat of prosecution without producing legal gender recognition.

Gender identity has no separate legal standing in Trinidad and Tobago. Rae Alibey, director of the Trinidad and Tobago Transgender Coalition, said in July 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised in law: gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation, and institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers.

Section 8 of the Immigration Act prohibits entry to Trinidad and Tobago for homosexual men and women who are not citizens. The provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice held that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize had violated the freedom of movement of the Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson, while clarifying that neither state may bar homosexual nationals of other CARICOM countries from entering, on the basis of treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas notwithstanding their domestic entry bans.

Trinidad and Tobago does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible to the rights and benefits available to opposite-sex couples. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property-dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting unequal treatment under current law and observing that, absent agreement, the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to divide property after dissolution of such a union.

The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected the addition of sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution, a decision announced at a special convention on 23 August 2024. Dr Angelique Nixon of CAISO said the community had been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection.

There is no hate-crime category in Trinidad and Tobago's legislation, a gap identified publicly by Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne in June 2024. A Newsday editorial of June 2024 recorded almost half a dozen Grindr-related attacks in recent months. In November 2024 police warned that criminals were creating fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two separate incidents reported in a single week.

The 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018, states that there are no special facilities in the Trinidad and Tobago penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities. Housing of a trans prisoner therefore rests on a sentencing judge's recommendation to prison authorities, with no dedicated facility behind it. The Protocol directs courts to refer to intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress.
tangentialFactors:
Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament on 17 June 2016 that the state must protect all citizens regardless of whom they sleep with, while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws. That stance predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling and is recorded here as the reform-refusal position of the time.

A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed rights or equality could be denied on the basis of sexual orientation. The figure is a 2009 attitudinal measure of the general population, not a current measure of attitudes toward trans people.

A 2012 travel and culture profile of the islands stated that homosexuality was illegal and that the laws were mostly ignored in practice. That statement of the law predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling and does not describe current law.
localsOnly:
The Trinidad and Tobago Transgender Coalition, directed by Rae Alibey, has called for national discussions and attitudinal research as prerequisites to recognition of gender identity, which remains absent from law as of July 2024.

CAISO was founded to encourage public discussion and legislative protections following the 2009 University of West Indies attitudinal research. Its spokesperson, Dr Angelique Nixon, publicly criticised the August 2024 constitutional-review decision to exclude sexual-orientation protections.

The Silver Lining Foundation works to end bullying against LGBTQ youth. A Newsday editorial of June 2024 argued that the absence of a hate-crime category in legislation must be closed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2018 Gender Equality Protocol has been implemented in practice, and how trans prisoners are in fact housed, is not documented in this inventory beyond the Protocol's own text.

Enforcement of Section 8 of the Immigration Act against non-citizen gay and lesbian arrivals is not known; no documented instance of its application appears in the sources.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator and a defined period appears in this inventory, so no trans-specific rate can be stated. The documented incidents are the Grindr-related attacks of 2024, counted in raw numbers only: almost half a dozen in the months before June 2024, and two in one week in November 2024.

Whether the criminal provisions struck down in 2018 have been replaced by any provision affecting trans people specifically is not sourced here.
